html:
Elam was an ancient civilisation in south-west Iran, centred on the lowland city of Susa and the highland city of Anshan, which lasted from about 2700 BCE until it was absorbed into the Persian Empire around 539 BCE. For more than two thousand years it was Mesopotamia's great neighbour and rival to the east.

The Elamites spoke a language unrelated to any other known language. They had their own scripts, Proto-Elamite and Linear Elamite, before they adopted cuneiform.

Elam was often at war with the states of Mesopotamia:

  • The Sumerian cities and then the Akkadian Empire fought and at times ruled parts of it.
  • In 2004 BCE the Elamites sacked Ur and ended Ur III, the last Sumerian state.
  • In the twelfth century BCE an Elamite king raided Babylonia and carried home famous monuments as trophies, among them the stele of the Code of Hammurabi, which was found at Susa in 1901.

The thirteenth century BCE ziggurat of Chogha Zanbil is the best surviving monument of Middle Elam.

Elam's last long struggle was with Assyria. Around 647 BCE the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal sacked Susa and boasted of salting its fields. Elam never fully recovered. The Persians of Anshan, under Cyrus, rose in its old lands, and Susa became a capital of the Achaemenid Empire. Elamite lived on for a while as a language of Persian government, used on thousands of clay tablets at Persepolis.
